items.prompt: What is the name for the stage of life from birth to about two years old?

options.label: Adolescence
options.feedback: Adolescence is the teenage years, not the first two years of life.

options.label: Childhood
options.feedback: Childhood generally covers the years after infancy, starting around age two or three, not the very first period.

options.label: Infancy
options.feedback: Infancy is the first two years after birth, the stage when a baby grows fastest and learns to sit, crawl, and walk.

options.label: Puberty
options.feedback: Puberty is the stage when the body changes to become sexually mature, which happens later, during adolescence.

items.ok_line: Infancy covers the first two years after birth.
items.ko_line: That is a later stage, not the first one.
items.exp_text: Infancy is the stage of life from birth to about two years old. During this time, a baby grows very quickly and develops basic skills like lifting its head, rolling over, sitting up, and eventually walking.

items.prompt: Which body part grows the fastest during early childhood?

options.label: The head
options.feedback: The head grows fastest early on because the brain is already developing rapidly, so it needs a bigger skull to protect it.

options.label: The legs
options.feedback: Legs grow fastest later, during the adolescent growth spurt, not in early childhood.

options.label: The hands
options.feedback: Hands and feet grow quickly during adolescence, not especially in early childhood.

options.label: The arms
options.feedback: Arms grow steadily but not as fast as the head in the first years of life.

items.ok_line: The head outpaces all other parts early on.
items.ko_line: That part grows quickly at another stage of life.
items.exp_text: In early childhood, the head grows faster than any other part of the body. This is because the brain is already busy developing, so the skull must expand quickly to keep up. Other parts, like legs and arms, catch up later.

items.prompt: What are a young child's first set of teeth called?

options.label: Permanent teeth
options.feedback: Permanent teeth replace the first set and come in later, starting around age six.

options.label: Molar teeth
options.feedback: Molars are specific back teeth, not the name for the whole first set.

options.label: Canine teeth
options.feedback: Canines are pointed teeth, one type among the first set, not the name for all of them.

options.label: Baby teeth
options.feedback: Baby teeth, also called milk teeth or deciduous teeth, are the first set that appear during infancy and early childhood.

items.ok_line: Baby teeth are the first teeth a child gets.
items.ko_line: That is not the name for the entire first set.
items.exp_text: The first set of teeth are called baby teeth. They start to come through the gums around six months of age and are gradually replaced by permanent teeth during childhood.

items.prompt: During the toddler years, what does a child learn to do that requires balance and coordination?

options.label: Read aloud
options.feedback: Reading develops later, around age five or six, and does not depend on physical balance.

options.label: Walk
options.feedback: Walking is the key skill of toddlerhood, and it requires the child to balance on two legs and coordinate many muscles.

options.label: Write letters
options.feedback: Writing letters comes much later, in school age, and involves fine motor skills, not whole-body balance.

options.label: Ride a bicycle
options.feedback: Riding a bicycle usually comes in later childhood, after walking is well established.

items.ko_line: That skill usually appears at a later age.
items.exp_text: During the toddler years, a child learns to walk. This takes practice because walking upright requires the brain, muscles, and bones to work together to keep the body balanced on two feet.

items.prompt: What is the name for the growth spurt that happens around ages 10 to 14 in girls and slightly later in boys?

options.label: Infant growth spurt
options.feedback: That spurt happens right after birth, not during the pre-teen years.

options.label: Childhood plateau
options.feedback: A plateau means no growth spurt; that term describes a steady period, not a rapid one.

options.label: Adolescent growth spurt
options.feedback: The adolescent growth spurt is the rapid increase in height that occurs during puberty, usually earlier in girls than in boys.

options.label: Senile growth spurt
options.feedback: Senile refers to old age, where growth does not speed up but actually stops.

items.ok_line: That is the adolescent growth spurt.
items.ko_line: That spurt happens at a different stage of life.
items.exp_text: The adolescent growth spurt is the rapid increase in height that happens around ages 10 to 14 in girls and a bit later in boys, driven by hormones. It is the fastest growth since infancy.

items.prompt: What is the soft, flexible material called that covers the ends of bones in a growing child?

options.label: Ligament
options.feedback: A ligament connects bone to bone, but it is not a covering for the bone ends.

options.label: Tendon
options.feedback: A tendon attaches muscle to bone, but it is not the covering of the bone ends.

options.label: Marrow
options.feedback: Marrow is the soft tissue inside the middle of a bone, not the outer covering of the ends.

options.label: Cartilage
options.feedback: Cartilage is the flexible, rubbery material that covers the ends of bones, allowing joints to move smoothly and helping bones grow longer.

items.ok_line: Cartilage caps the ends of bones.
items.ko_line: That structure does not cover bone ends.
items.exp_text: Cartilage is the smooth, flexible tissue that covers the ends of bones where they meet at joints. In children, it also acts as a growth plate, where new bone forms to make the bone longer.

items.prompt: At what age do most children begin to lose their baby teeth?

options.label: About age six
options.feedback: Around age six, the roots of baby teeth dissolve and the teeth fall out, making room for permanent teeth.

options.label: About age three
options.feedback: At age three, baby teeth are just coming in fully, not falling out yet.

options.label: About age twelve
options.feedback: By age twelve, most baby teeth have already been replaced; losing them starts earlier.

options.label: About age eighteen
options.feedback: At eighteen, permanent teeth are already in place; baby teeth are long gone.

items.ok_line: Most children lose their first baby tooth around six.
items.ko_line: That age is not when baby teeth typically fall out.
items.exp_text: Most children start to lose their baby teeth around age six. The roots of the baby tooth get dissolved, so the tooth becomes loose and falls out, and the permanent tooth underneath pushes up.

items.prompt: What are the new, larger teeth that come in behind the baby teeth called?

options.label: Milk teeth
options.feedback: Milk teeth are the same as baby teeth, the first set, not the replacements.

options.label: Permanent teeth
options.feedback: Permanent teeth are the adult set that replace baby teeth and do not fall out naturally.

options.label: Wisdom teeth
options.feedback: Wisdom teeth are a specific type of permanent molars that appear in late teens or twenties, not all new teeth.

options.label: Temporary teeth
options.feedback: Temporary teeth are baby teeth, which are meant to fall out; permanent ones are not temporary.

items.ko_line: That name belongs to a different set of teeth.
items.exp_text: The new teeth that replace baby teeth are called permanent teeth because they are meant to last the rest of a person's life. They are larger and stronger than baby teeth and start appearing around age six.

items.prompt: What happens to a baby's height and weight during the first year of life?

options.label: They stay almost the same
options.feedback: A baby grows very rapidly, so staying the same is not correct for the first year.

options.label: They double only in weight
options.feedback: Weight typically triples, not just doubles, and height also increases significantly.

options.label: They increase rapidly
options.feedback: In the first year, a baby usually triples its birth weight and grows about twenty-five centimeters, a very rapid increase.

options.label: They decrease then increase
options.feedback: A newborn does not lose height or weight overall; growth is continuous in the first year.

items.ok_line: Babies grow very quickly in year one.
items.ko_line: Stable or dropping measurements are not typical of infancy.
items.exp_text: During the first year, a baby grows at its fastest rate after birth. Weight usually triples, and length increases by about half of birth length. This rapid growth slows down later in childhood.

items.prompt: What is the name for the way a child's body proportions change as it grows, with the head becoming smaller relative to the rest of the body?

options.label: Shrinking
options.feedback: Shrinking means becoming smaller in absolute size, but the head does not shrink; it just becomes a smaller fraction of total height.

options.label: Stretching
options.feedback: Stretching describes the limbs lengthening, but it does not capture the head-to-body ratio change.

options.label: Maturing
options.feedback: Maturing is a general term, not the specific name for this change in body proportions.

options.label: Allometric growth
options.feedback: Allometric growth is the scientific term for body parts growing at different rates, so the head becomes proportionally smaller as the rest catches up.

items.ko_line: Those words do not name this specific pattern.
items.exp_text: Allometric growth means different parts of the body grow at different speeds. For example, the head grows quickly early on but slowly later, so by adulthood it is much smaller relative to the total body height than it was in infancy.
